approach_variants.name: Fisher Creek to the lake camp, over the ridge onto the Banded Glacier
camps: Fisher Creek lake camp below the Banded Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Two ways in, and which one you use depends on whether SR-20 is open. The always-open option is the Thunder Creek trail from Colonial Creek Campground near 1,200 ft for about nine miles to the Fisher Creek trail junction, then the Fisher Creek trail about three miles — past a good log bridge with a handrail — to a lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. Roughly thirteen miles one way. The shorter option is Easy Pass from SR-20 near milepost 151, over the pass at 6,500 ft and down into Fisher Basin, about ten miles, but the trailhead is gated by the highway's seasonal closure.

From the lake camp, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — which may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section. Drop onto the Banded Glacier on the far side and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col.

The last two thirds of this route is sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding, and the scree below the glacier is described as moving like a Newtonian fluid: much easier to ascend than to descend. Party size in this NPS zone is capped at six.
hazards: Major crevasse crossed on a narrow snow bridge on the Banded Glacier; snow bridge collapse near Christmas Tree Col
Christmas Tree Col may need a rope for steep snow or a short glacier section
Talus lying on bullet-hard glacier ice is treacherous, especially in a whiteout descent
Cliff bands above the lake camp; loose chossy rock on the summit ridge; rockfall in approach gullies
Sustained off-trail goat-path route-finding on the upper two-thirds; scree much harder to descend
Heavy mosquitoes in the lake basin through June and July
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The critical transition is a negative test: gain the northeast ridge on solid rock at about 8,800 ft rather than attempting the summit block directly from the glacier. That is the base of the climbing and it is the single thing this route can get wrong. If you are trying to climb off the ice straight at the summit, you have skipped the transition — cross the glacier until you can step onto solid rock on the ridge, and only then start up.

Getting there is a sequence of two cols and they are different things. First, from the lake camp near 5,160 ft, climb south-southeast to a low point on the ridge — sometimes called Christmas Tree Col — and drop over it onto the Banded Glacier. Second, ascend the Banded to the Banded-Douglas Col, which is literally the saddle between the two named glaciers. A col you crossed to reach ice, and a col you reached by climbing ice, are not the same feature.

So the question that settles your position in fog is which glacier is under you: this route travels between two named glaciers, so if you can identify which one you are standing on, you know which stage you are at. The Banded is the one you drop onto from the ridge above camp; the Douglas is on the far side of the col above.

And all three Logan routes end on the same 300 ft of class 3-4 summit block, so the summit confirms nothing. What distinguishes them is entirely below: this one comes from Fisher Creek and a lake camp; the Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder; the Fremont Glacier route comes from Park Creek Pass on the other side of the mountain.

Watch the scree below the glacier on the way up with the descent in mind — it is unstable enough that parties note it climbs far better than it downclimbs.

bivy.notes: Reached via the Fisher Creek Trail fork off the Thunder Creek Trail (~9 miles in); the standard overnight camp below the Banded Glacier.

approach_variants.notes: From the Easy Pass Trailhead on SR-20, over the 6,500 ft pass into Fisher Basin, then down the Fisher Creek trail to the lake outlet and the same camp as the Thunder Creek way.
hazards: Gated trailhead tied to SR-20 seasonal closure limits when this way in is open
Crossing of a 6,500 ft pass into Fisher Basin before dropping to the lake camp
Christmas Tree Col may need a rope for steep snow; snow bridge collapse risk on the Banded Glacier

approach_logistics.trailheadDirection: From the Thunder Creek trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20 (~1,200 ft)

waypoints.name: Thunder Creek Trailhead (Colonial Creek Campground, Hwy 20)
waypoints.note: Overnight stays in the park need a North Cascades backcountry permit, reserved on Recreation.gov or picked up at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20, the North Cascades Highway, to Colonial Creek Campground near milepost 130 on Diablo Lake. The Thunder Creek trail starts at the south end of the campground, at about 1,200 ft. Overnight stays in the park need a North Cascades backcountry permit.

waypoints.name: Lake camp below the Banded Glacier
waypoints.note: Unnamed lake near 5,160 ft on Logan's north side; the usual high camp for the Banded Glacier. Mosquitoes are heavy in June and July, and getting around the lake can be awkward.
waypoints.directions: Take the Thunder Creek Trail about 10 miles to the Fisher Creek Trail, then the Fisher Creek Trail about 3 miles to just past a handrailed log bridge over the stream that drains the lake. Leave the trail and follow that drainage up to the lake at about 5,160 ft.

waypoints.name: Mount Logan summit
waypoints.note: Gain the northeast ridge on solid rock near 8,800 ft rather than climbing straight off the glacier at the summit block. Reverse the route to descend; the scree below the glacier is much harder going down than up.
waypoints.directions: From the lake, climb south-southeast up talus and snowfields to Christmas Tree Col, an orange-brown notch that is hard to spot from the lake. Drop onto the Banded Glacier and ascend it to the Banded-Douglas Col, then gain the northeast ridge on rock near 8,800 ft and scramble the Class 3-4 summit block.

bivy.name: Fisher Creek lake camp below the Banded Glacier
bivy.notes: Reached via the Fisher Creek Trail fork off the Thunder Creek Trail (~9 miles in); the standard overnight camp below the Banded Glacier.
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit — reserve via Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center

bivy.name: Neve Camp
bivy.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the bugs are heavy through midsummer. Nothing about it is alpine, which is exactly its function on a corridor where the climbing is fifteen or more miles in.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek runs beside the camp and is reliable all season.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round. Issued at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, or emailed in advance against a reservation. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through recreation.gov (spring lottery, then a general on-sale in late April); the rest is held for walk-up and can only be claimed the day before or day of your start.
bivy.capacity: Small forested camp, reported at roughly five tent spots, spread out enough that parties are not on top of each other. Confirm the count and per-site party limit when the permit is issued.

approach: Follow Thunder Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground (SR-20 MP130) about 9 miles to the Fisher Creek Trail junction, then Fisher Creek Trail about 3 miles to a lake camp near 5,160 ft below the Banded Glacier. When SR-20 is open, the shorter way in (about 10 miles one way) starts at the Easy Pass Trailhead near milepost 151, crosses the 6,500-ft pass and drops into Fisher Basin, then follows the Fisher Creek trail down to the same lake outlet.

itinerary.cal: Easy Pass Trail typically isn't snow-free until July. Highway 20 access to the Easy Pass Trailhead is seasonal — typically open mid-April/May through early December, but exact dates vary by year and by winter storm damage (confirm via WSDOT); the trailhead sits inside the MP134-171 winter closure zone. The longer Thunder Creek Trailhead alternate is open year-round if Easy Pass is still gated. An NPS backcountry permit is required for the lake camp.

days.note: Hike the Easy Pass Trail up and over the pass (~6,600 ft), descend into the Fisher Creek drainage, then leave trail to reach a basin lake camp near the toe of the Banded Glacier — expect a sketchy log-bridge creek crossing and boggy ground near the lake.
days.title: Approach to Banded Glacier basin camp
days.objective: Reach the lake camp below the Banded Glacier

days.note: A long alpine day: climb loose talus and a rockfall-prone gully to the obscure, hard-to-spot Christmas Tree Col, drop into the Banded Glacier basin, rope up and stay climber's-left of the crevasses to the Banded-Douglas col, then follow a loose Class 2-3 ridge to the summit before reversing the entire route.
days.title: Summit via Christmas Tree Col and the Banded Glacier

schedule.label: Reach Christmas Tree Col
schedule.detail: Not obvious from the lake — look for an orange-brown notch above the snowfields.

schedule.label: Rope up on the Banded Glacier
schedule.detail: Stay climber's-left to avoid the worst crevasses.

schedule.label: Summit
schedule.detail: Via the Banded-Douglas col and NE ridge.

days.objective: Reach the true summit and return to camp

days.note: Reverse the approach over Easy Pass back to the trailhead.
days.title: Hike out
days.objective: Return to the Easy Pass Trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A strenuous 3-day, ~29-mile round trip (~12,500 ft gain) via Easy Pass; the crux is a very long (12+ hr) summit day through the loose, hard-to-find Christmas Tree Col and a roped glacier crossing. Very strong parties have linked the whole route car-to-car in a single ~13.5 hr day, but that is an outlier push, not the standard plan.

gaps: Ridge col name ('possibly Christmas Tree Col') is uncertain in available sources
29 mi / 12,500 ft stats come from a single detailed trip report, not a guidebook average
